analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal license to own guns, bans assault weapons and silencers, and expands background checks, waiting periods, and storage rules.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Sen. Elizabeth Warren with 3 Democratic cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require every person who buys or owns a firearm or ammunition to hold a federal license, obtained at age 21 or older after a background check, safety training, and photograph. It would extend background checks to virtually all gun transfers, lengthen the waiting period to 7 business days, ban assault weapons, large-capacity magazines, gun silencers, and untraceable 'ghost' guns, raise the minimum purchase age to 21 for all firearms, require safe storage, and fund community violence intervention programs. It would also strip gun makers of their protection from some lawsuits and raise federal excise taxes on firearms.
analysis.who_benefits: People exposed to gun violence, including victims of domestic abuse, families at risk of suicide by firearm, and residents of communities with high rates of shootings. Domestic violence victims gain because dating partners and people convicted of misdemeanor stalking would be barred from buying guns. Community organizations gain new grant funding for violence intervention and research.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People exposed to gun violence and domestic abuse

how_it_helps.text: Requires a federal firearm owner's license to purchase or possess any firearm or ammunition, available only to people 21 or older who pass a background check, complete safety training with written and firing tests, and submit a photograph; states with substantially similar licensing programs can substitute their own.
Extends background checks to nearly all firearm transfers, including private sales, and sets a minimum 7-business-day waiting period before a sale can be completed.

Bans new sales of semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity ammunition magazines, bans firearm silencers, and bans untraceable and undetectable firearms, with buy-back programs funded through existing law-enforcement grants.

Expands federal gun prohibitions to cover dating partners and people convicted of misdemeanor stalking, closes the so-called 'boyfriend loophole,' and bars people with outstanding arrest warrants from buying guns.

Creates federal extreme risk protection orders — court orders allowing family members or police to ask a judge to temporarily remove firearms from someone posing a danger to themselves or others — and funds grants for states and tribes that adopt their own versions, with due-process hearings and no filing fees.

Requires secure storage of firearms around minors or ineligible residents, with civil penalties and up to 5 years' imprisonment if a prohibited person or minor obtains an improperly stored gun, and directs the Consumer Product Safety Commission to set safety standards for gun locks and safes.

Raises the minimum purchase age to 21 for all firearms and ammunition, with exceptions for employment, ranching and farming, target practice and hunting under written parental consent, and military service.

Repeals the 2005 law shielding gun manufacturers and dealers from most civil lawsuits, removes firearms' special exclusion from consumer product safety laws, raises federal excise taxes on firearms, and funds community violence intervention grants and firearms research.

analysis.who_pays: Gun owners, who would need a federal license, safety training, background checks for nearly every transfer, and compliant storage; and the firearms industry, which would face an assault weapons and silencer ban, a higher excise tax, dealer inspections and record-keeping requirements, employee background checks, and exposure to civil lawsuits that current law blocks.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun owners, gun manufacturers, and gun dealers

drawbacks.text: The licensing system applies to every firearm and ammunition purchase and to possession itself, so millions of current and prospective gun owners with no criminal record would face training, testing, background-check, and licensing requirements before and after the two-year effective date.

Even semiautomatic assault weapons owned before the ban could only be transferred after a licensed dealer runs a background check, and possessing a banned weapon or silencer after the effective date carries criminal penalties, which falls hardest on owners unfamiliar with the new rules.

Compliance costs — training courses, license applications, safes or locks meeting new federal standards, and a 7-business-day wait on purchases — would fall on individual buyers, and the licensing apparatus (an ATF-run database, annual background investigations of every license holder, and court 'unsuitability' petitions) is a substantial administrative expansion whose execution would depend on regulators.

Opponents argue the sweep of the restrictions — a near-universal license to own, a 21 purchase age, and bans on popular categories of firearms — burdens the rights of law-abiding owners more than necessary to reduce violence; supporters of narrower measures note the bill went far beyond the policies Congress has previously passed with bipartisan support.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets gun deaths — homicides, domestic killings, suicides, and mass shootings — with a package of measures most of which are already in force in some states, and the public-health case for reducing firearm deaths is strong. The costs are real but limited: millions of lawful owners would absorb licensing, training, waiting, and storage burdens, and the industry would bear a genuine financial hit from the bans, taxes, and lost lawsuit shield. The main design criticism is scale: the bill bundles incremental, widely supported policies like background-check and domestic-violence fixes with sweeping bans and licensing that have never come close to passage in Congress, making the whole package easier to oppose as one unit.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced on December 5, 2023 and referred the same day to the Senate Finance Committee, which took no action; the bill died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025 without a hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the Gun Violence Prevention and Community Safety Act of 2023 in the Senate on December 5, 2023, joined by Sens. Booker, Markey, and Hirono.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day it was introduced.
No further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — appears in the action history through the end of the 118th Congress.

The bill's full text laid out a federal firearms licensing system, universal background checks with a 7-day waiting period, an assault weapons and silencer ban, extreme risk protection orders, storage requirements, and a repeal of the gun industry's civil liability shield.
The bill ended with only 3 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no Republican support on record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun manufacturers and dealers are better off: because the bill never moved, the industry keeps the 2005 liability shield, current excise tax rates, and its existing sales categories, and current gun owners face no new licensing or storage requirements.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Democrats and the bill's only 3 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and major gun legislation in this Congress split almost entirely by party.

industries.note: The bill bans future sales of assault weapons, large-capacity magazines, silencers, and untraceable guns, raises excise taxes, subjects firearms to consumer product safety laws for the first time, and repeals the 2005 law that shields manufacturers from most civil suits. Its gain to the public runs through fewer deaths, which comes directly out of the industry's sales and legal exposure.

Dealers would face mandatory inspections, employee background checks, enhanced record-keeping, limits on multiple sales, verification of buyers' licenses, and a repealed cap on ATF inspections. The bill treats dealer practices, including losses and thefts, as a driver of gun trafficking.

industries.industry: Gun owners as a concentrated interest
industries.note: Owners would bear licensing, training, waiting-period, and secure-storage costs and would lose access to banned firearm categories, while also gaining from a licensing system that keeps guns away from people courts find dangerous. Millions of lawful owners would feel the burden directly.

Federal safety standards for firearm locks and safes would create a compliance-driven market for certified storage products as every owner becomes legally required to secure guns around minors and prohibited residents.
The bill authorizes grant programs for street-level violence intervention and for firearms research, channels that rely on local community organizations to deliver the services.
